## What it does

1inch is a decentralized exchange (DEX) aggregator. When you swap tokens, it splits the order across multiple liquidity sources to get a better average rate than any single exchange offers.

## The key insight

Sergej Kunz and Anton Bukov built the first prototype in 56 hours at ETHGlobal New York in May 2019. The insight: on any single DEX, a large order moves the price against you (slippage). Splitting the same order across three DEXes with different liquidity pools produces a better average rate.

The math is simple. If exchange A holds 60% of the liquidity and exchange B holds 40%, sending 60% of your trade to A and 40% to B minimizes total slippage. The hard part is computing that split in real time across dozens of pools with changing reserves.

## How it works

The system has three layers.

**Routing.** Given a token pair and an amount, find all available pools (Uniswap, SushiSwap, Curve, and others). For each pool, compute the output amount given the input. Uniswap-style pools use a constant-product formula: x times y equals k.

**Splitting.** Decide how to divide the input across pools. The original algorithm split the order iteratively, testing each split against the others. Later versions use on-chain optimization.

**Execution.** Submit one transaction that performs all the sub-swaps atomically. If any leg fails, the whole transaction reverts. The user signs once; the contract handles the routing.

The aggregator takes a small fee (0.1% to 0.3%) from the price improvement it delivers. If it cannot beat the best single venue, it routes there instead.

## Build something similar

Start with two Uniswap V2-style pools for the same token pair, each with different reserves.

Write a function that, given an input amount, computes the output for pool A, pool B, and three split ratios (all A, 50/50, all B). Print the results.

The split that wins depends on the reserves. With equal reserves, 50/50 wins. With 80/20 reserves, the split roughly matches. This is the entire insight in ten lines of code.

Then add a third pool. The number of split combinations grows, but the principle holds: more pools means more opportunities to beat any single venue.

## Sources

Origin and prototype details are from the 1inch press room and blog posts linked in the evidence field.

A satellite dataset becomes useful when it answers a question with a date attached. "Is the soil wet enough this week" is a better product than a soil-moisture map.

## What it is

Account Kit was a Facebook login product that verified a phone number without sending an SMS. Early tests reported a 97% success rate.

## The problem

SMS verification fails for reasons the developer cannot see: delayed messages, wrong country codes, shared phones, and carrier filtering. Each failure is a user who does not get into the app.

## What makes it interesting

It came out of the Facebook Seattle Platform team hackathon in 2016. The interesting choice is the constraint: prove the number without relying on a text message arriving.

## What you can learn

When a verification step has a high failure rate, the fix may be a different channel rather than a better error message. Measure the step, then remove its weakest dependency.

## Limitations of this analysis

The record does not explain the verification mechanism, the markets it targeted, or how the 97% figure was measured.

## What it does

AdSense places contextual text and display ads on websites. Publishers paste a snippet of JavaScript; the script requests ads that match the page content and earns revenue when visitors click.

## The key insight

Susan Wojcicki proposed the idea in 2002 as a Google 20% project. The problem: Google had AdWords (advertisers bidding on keywords) but no way to place those ads on the millions of small websites that had content but no sales force. AdSense closed that gap by automating the match between page content and ad inventory.

The revenue number tells the story. Within two years of launch in June 2003, AdSense generated roughly 15% of Google's total revenue.

## How it works

**Content analysis.** The script sends the page URL (and sometimes extracted text) to Google's servers. An algorithm determines the page's topics: the words, the category, the context.

**Ad selection.** Google matches those topics against keywords that advertisers are bidding on. Advertisers set bids per keyword in AdWords; AdSense surfaces the highest-bidding ads relevant to the page.

**Auction.** Multiple ads compete for the slot. Google runs a second-price auction: the winner pays one cent more than the second-highest bidder. This keeps bids honest.

**Rendering.** The script receives ad code (HTML and CSS) and injects it into the page. The publisher never sees the auction logic; they get a div that fills with ads.

**Revenue share.** Google keeps a percentage (reported around 68%) and pays the publisher the rest (32%). The exact split is not public and has changed over time.

## Build something similar

Build a page that displays a sponsored link based on the page's own content.

Start with a static mapping: define five topics (cooking, finance, travel, fitness, technology) and one ad creative for each. Write a function that reads the page title and tags, scores each topic by word overlap, and picks the highest.

This gives you the core loop: analyze content, select an ad, render it. The difference between this and production AdSense is scale (millions of pages, real-time auction) and quality (advertisers actually paying).

Then add a simple auction: two advertisers bidding on the same keyword, winner pays second-highest bid plus one cent. This is the AdWords mechanism.

## Sources

Origin and revenue figures are documented in Wikipedia's 20% Project article, linked in the evidence field.
projects.description: Contextual advertising platform for publishers. Generated approximately 15% of Google revenue within two years of launch.

evidence.supports: Google 20% project origin, Susan Wojcicki, revenue contribution

projects.key_idea: Match text ads to page content automatically, so publishers earn revenue without selling inventory themselves.
projects.learn_from: A 20% time project won because it solved a real distribution problem: thousands of small sites had content but no sales team.

## What it is

Airocide is a line of air purifiers built on technology developed for spacecraft life support. The core process is catalytic oxidation, which breaks down organic gases rather than trapping them in a filter.

## How the experience works

Air passes through a catalyst bed, where volatile organic compounds are oxidized. The output is carbon dioxide and water vapor. Because the catalyst is not consumed, it does not need the replacement schedule of a particulate filter.

## What makes it interesting

The product is a technology transfer: research paid for by a space program became a consumer appliance. NASA's spinoff programs exist to make that path visible and repeatable.

## What you can learn

Dual-use research can produce a consumer product when the operating constraint is shared. A spacecraft and a sealed room both need air that does not accumulate trace gases.

## Limitations of this analysis

The record does not document the license, the underlying studies, or independent performance testing. Claims about health effects are outside what the linked source establishes.

## What it does

Cycles is a physically based render engine inside Blender. It traces light paths from the camera through the scene and produces images where reflections, shadows, and indirect light come from the same simulation instead of separate fakes.

## The key insight

Rasterizers approximate light with shortcuts: shadow maps, reflection probes, ambient terms. Cycles does the opposite. It samples paths and averages them. Noise is not a bug, it is the visible cost of sampling, and it falls as the sample count rises.

That choice makes the engine predictable. A material that looks right in one scene tends to look right in another, because the same physical rules apply.

## How it works

A path tracer shoots rays from the camera. At each surface it chooses a bounce direction, weights the contribution, and continues. When a ray reaches a light or the background, the path contributes to the pixel. Many paths per pixel produce the estimate.

Importance sampling decides where to send rays. Instead of sampling uniformly, the integrator samples directions that are likely to matter, such as toward a light or along a glossy lobe. Good sampling means fewer paths for the same noise level.

Acceleration structures make ray traversal practical. A bounding volume hierarchy groups geometry so a ray can skip most of the scene. Without it, every bounce would test every triangle.

Materials are node graphs compiled into shader code. The graph describes the surface, and the renderer evaluates it at each hit. Because the description is procedural, the same material works in Cycles and, where supported, in the real-time engine.

GPU rendering splits the same work across many cores. The integrator is data-parallel by design, which is why the same engine runs on CPU and GPU with different performance rather than different output.

## Build something similar

Write a path tracer for spheres and a plane. Camera ray, intersect, bounce, accumulate. Render at one sample per pixel and look at the noise.

Add importance sampling for the light. The image should get cleaner without more samples.

Then add one material property, such as roughness, and watch the highlight widen. The whole engine is an accumulation of these small physical decisions, which is why a minimal version teaches more than a feature-complete one.

## Sources

GSoC connection and project history are linked in the evidence field.

evidence.supports: GSoC connection, Brecht Van Lommel, 100+ Blender projects funded

projects.learn_from: A physically based core can ship inside an existing tool if the integration is one engine behind an existing interface.

## What it does

Buck is a build system for large codebases, built at Facebook for Android. It reads declarative build files, constructs a dependency graph, and executes independent work in parallel with caching.

## The key insight

The prototype came out of a Facebook hackathon in 2012 because the Android build had become the slowest part of the developer loop. The fix was not a faster compiler. It was removing hidden dependencies so that work could be parallelized and reused.

A build that recompiles the world on every change cannot be made fast by optimizing the compiler. It has to be restructured.

## How it works

Build files declare targets: a library, a binary, a test, each with sources, dependencies, and rules. The declarations are explicit, so the tool can compute the full graph without scanning the filesystem for implicit inputs.

From the graph, Buck derives the work. Independent nodes run concurrently. A node whose inputs and rule have not changed is skipped entirely, which is why incremental builds are fast even when the graph is large.

Caching extends the skip across machines. If a target's inputs hash to a known value, the output can be fetched instead of rebuilt. This turns a build into a lookup for most nodes and a compile for the few that changed.

Correctness depends on the dependency declarations being complete. An undeclared dependency produces a build that works locally and fails in a clean checkout, so the tool enforces strictness rather than tolerating implicit inputs.

For Android specifically, the system also split application packaging from code compilation. Resources and code can be updated independently, which shortens the install cycle during development.

## Build something similar

Write a build file format with three fields: inputs, outputs, and a command. Parse it into a graph.

Run the graph in topological order, skipping any node whose inputs are unchanged. Time a rebuild after touching one file. That number is the whole point of the tool.

Then add a content hash for each output and a cache directory keyed by hash. If a clean build can reuse entries from a previous one, you have the core of a modern build system.

## Sources

Facebook engineering writeup and hackathon origin are linked in the evidence field.
projects.description: Fast modular Android build system used at Facebook. Prototype built in one hackathon.

evidence.supports: Hack-a-Thona July 2012 prototype origin

projects.key_idea: Describe a build as a graph of declared targets, then execute and cache each node independently.
projects.learn_from: Find the bottleneck you can measure, then remove the mechanism that causes it. Build tools win on correctness and speed, not features.
projects.name: Buck

## What it is

Carousell is a mobile-first marketplace for secondhand goods. A seller photographs an item, adds a price, and publishes a listing in about a minute.

## The problem

Classifieds sites were built for desktop browsers and long forms. Selling a used phone required a camera, a cable, and patience, when the phone in the seller's pocket was already the best tool for the job.

## How the experience works

The listing flow starts with a photo and asks for the minimum: title, price, category. Buyers browse and message the seller. The short flow is the product.

## What makes it interesting

The team built the working demo in 54 hours at Startup Weekend Singapore in 2012, under the name SnapSell, and won first place. The name changed; the one-minute listing stayed.

## What you can learn

Removing steps from a listing flow increases supply, and supply is what makes a marketplace usable. The camera was the feature, not the form.

## Limitations of this analysis

The record covers the origin and the demo, not the trust and safety system or the payment model.

## What it does

Celebrate Pride let Facebook users apply a rainbow filter to their profile picture. It shipped in 72 hours around a hackathon and reached roughly 26 million users in its first weekend.

## The key insight

The feature is a filter, not a campaign site. It reused a surface every user already had, the profile photo, and changed one property of it. There was no new page to visit and no new account to create.

That is why it could spread in a weekend. The action was one tap, and the result was visible to everyone who looked at the profile.

## How it works

The client offers a toggle on the existing profile picture flow. Choosing it sends the image reference to a service that composites the overlay and returns a new image. The original photo stays intact, so the change is reversible.

The image work is the bottleneck. Millions of users applying the same overlay within hours means the compositing step has to be cheap and the result has to be cacheable. The overlay is a fixed asset, so the output can be produced once per photo and served from cache rather than recomputed per view.

Client support is the second constraint. The feature has to appear on every platform that shows a profile picture, which means the toggle and the result must be represented in the shared profile model rather than in one client's local state.

Timeboxing shaped the architecture. A 72-hour window rules out new infrastructure, so the team built on existing image and profile services. The constraint produced a simpler design than a greenfield build would have.

## Build something similar

Pick a surface every user already has, such as an avatar, a banner, or a display name. Add one reversible variant of it.

Precompute the variant as a static asset and serve it from cache. Then add the toggle to the shared user model so every client sees the same state.

Measure how long it takes a new user to reach the changed state. If it is more than a couple of taps, the feature is too expensive to spread.

## Sources

Engineering writeup, user count, and 72-hour timeline are linked in the evidence field.

## What it does

The Like button is a one-click signal of approval attached to posts, photos, pages, and eventually other sites. It turned a private bookmark-style action into a public, countable metric.

## The key insight

Justin Rosenstein built a prototype called "Props" at a Facebook internal hackathon in 2007. It sat unused for roughly two years. When it launched in 2009, the important decision was not the icon. It was scope: one bit of feedback, applied to everything, with the count visible to everyone.

A five-point rating would have carried more information and spread less. One bit is cheap to give, cheap to display, and comparable across objects of different kinds.

## How it works

On Facebook, a Like is a row in a social graph with a user, an object, and a type. Counting is a read over that edge set, which is why the number can be shown on every post without a separate counter to keep in sync.

Off the main site, the button ships as a small snippet that renders a cross-origin frame. The frame isolates the host page's CSS from Facebook's, and it carries the session needed to attribute the click. That isolation is why the same few lines of embed code work on a blog, a news site, and a product page.

Aggregation is the hard part. A popular page can produce far more writes than reads, and the count has to survive that ratio. Caching and precomputed totals absorb most of the load, with the exact value reconciled in the background.

The visual language mattered as much as the mechanism. A thumb, a count, and a consistent position trained users across unrelated sites. The button became recognizable before it became useful on any particular page.

## Build something similar

Add one-bit feedback to something you already run. A row with a user id, an object id, and a timestamp is enough.

Show the count next to the control, and make the control work on a second surface, such as an embed or a second client. The moment two surfaces share the same edge table, you have the core of the system.

Then measure the ratio of writes to reads on a popular item. That number decides whether you need a cache, a queue, or nothing at all.

## Sources

Origin and prototype details are linked in the evidence field.

## What it does

Figma Slides is a presentation tool built on Figma's design canvas. Teams design slides with the same tools they use for interfaces, then present them in the same file.

## The key insight

The team did not build a presentation editor from scratch. It built a slide layer on top of the editor that already existed: same canvas, same document, same multiplayer session, same component system.

That reuse set the schedule. The hackathon project at Figma's Maker Week in late 2023 became a shipped product in about two years, which is short for a new surface with its own editing model.

## How it works

A deck is a Figma document. Each slide is a frame, and the slide grid is a layout constraint over those frames rather than a separate data structure. Because slides are frames, every existing design tool works on them: auto layout, components, styles, images.

Editing is shared state. Multiple cursors and selections already work because the multiplayer layer operates on the document, not on a screen. Adding a presenter view means adding a way to read the same document, not a new sync protocol.

The slide-specific parts are narrow: a grid that arranges frames in order, a presenter mode that advances through them, and transitions between them. Those are additions on top of the existing model rather than a parallel implementation.

The hard part is the constraint. A design canvas is free-form, and a slide deck is sequential. The grid has to enforce order and alignment without taking away the freedom that makes the canvas useful.

## Build something similar

Take an editor you already have, or a simple canvas with draggable rectangles. Add a grid that arranges frames in reading order.

Add a presenter mode that shows one frame at a time and advances on a key press. That is a slide deck.

Then add one feature that only makes sense because the frames are editable, such as a shared component for a footer. The product becomes more than a slideshow at the point where the design tools carry over.

## Sources

## What it does

Friday Night Funkin' is a rhythm game where you press arrow keys in time with music while a opponent sings against you. It started as a Ludum Dare 47 entry in October 2020 and became a viral hit with a large modding scene.

## The key insight

Rhythm games have a small mechanical core: notes arrive on a timeline, the player hits them within a timing window, and the game scores the difference. The jam build implemented that core and wrapped it in characters and music.

The team open-sourced the game. The chart format and the asset layout were readable, so modders could add songs and characters without reverse-engineering the engine. Most of the game's long tail came from that decision.

## How it works

Audio position is the clock. The game tracks the current playback time of the song and spawns notes whose timestamps fall inside the visible window. Judgement compares the time of the key press against the note's timestamp and assigns a rating from the offset.

A chart is a sequence of notes with timestamps, lanes, and lengths for holds. Splitting the chart from the song file means a new track is data, not code.

The engine is written in Haxe and targets multiple platforms through OpenFL. That choice gives one codebase for desktop and web, which matters when the audience arrives through a browser game portal.

Modding works because assets and charts are loaded from a known directory structure. A mod is a folder with a song, a chart, and sprites. The game reads the folder and plays it, with no plugin API required.

## Build something similar

Build the clock first. Load an audio file, display its playback time, and draw a marker that moves with it.

Add notes with timestamps. Spawn each note a fixed number of seconds before its time and move it toward a hit line. On a key press, compare the current time to the nearest note's timestamp and print the offset.

Then move the notes into a JSON file. When you can add a song by editing data instead of code, you have the same extension point that made modding possible.

## Sources

Ludum Dare origin, repository, and developer devlog are linked in the evidence field.

## What it does

Gephi is an open-source tool for exploring and visualizing graphs. You load a network, run a layout, color and size nodes by a metric, and filter the result interactively.

## The key insight

Most graph tools at the time produced static output: compute a layout, render an image, publish it. Gephi made layout interactive. You can start a force-directed layout, watch it settle, stop it, and change a parameter while looking at the result.

That changes the work. Exploration becomes a loop of adjusting and observing rather than a batch job with a preview at the end.

## How it works

The data model is a graph with nodes, edges, and attributes, plus a separate attribute table. Metrics such as degree, betweenness, and modularity are computed into columns that can drive visual properties.

Layout algorithms are iterative. Force-directed layouts treat edges as springs and nodes as repelling charges, then repeatedly move each node by the net force. The result is a position for every node, refined over many steps rather than solved once.

Rendering is the constraint. A graph with hundreds of thousands of edges cannot be drawn naively at interactive rates, so the view culls, batches, and uses the GPU for the heavy drawing. The layout runs in the background while the view stays responsive.

Importers are the adoption path. Gephi reads edge lists, matrix formats, and database queries, because a visualization tool is only as useful as the data it can open. Google Summer of Code support from 2009 to 2011 funded much of that connector and plugin work.

## Build something similar

Load a small edge list and compute a force-directed layout yourself. Springs for edges, repulsion for all pairs, and a damping factor. Run a hundred iterations and draw the result.

Then make it interactive: a slider for repulsion, a button to stop and restart. The tool becomes useful when you can see the effect of a parameter without re-running a pipeline.

Add one metric, such as degree, and map it to node size. That single mapping turns a picture of a graph into an explanation of it.

## Sources

GSoC history and project description are linked in the evidence field.

## What it is

Getaround is a peer-to-peer car rental marketplace. Owners list cars by the hour or day; renters book and unlock them through the app.

Car sharing usually requires a company fleet and a physical key handoff. Peer-to-peer rental has a trust problem and an access problem: the owner is not there to hand over the key.

A hardware kit installed in the car connects the vehicle to the platform. After a booking, the renter unlocks the car from the phone, so the owner never has to meet them.

The company launched at TechCrunch Disrupt NYC 2011 and won the Startup Battlefield that day. It later listed on the NYSE, then announced a wind-down in 2026. That arc is unusually complete for an archive entry: weekend stage, public company, ending.

Marketplaces with a physical access problem need hardware, not just software. The install and recovery path for that hardware is part of the product, not an accessory to it.

## Limitations of this analysis

The record does not cover the kit's design, the insurance model, or the reasons behind the 2026 wind-down.

Google News is an aggregator that groups articles by story and links readers to the publishers.

## What it does

Grafana renders time-series data from multiple backends into dashboards. It connects to Prometheus, InfluxDB, Elasticsearch, and dozens of other data sources through a plugin model.

## The key insight

Torkel Odegaard built it during a Christmas hackathon in 2013 because he wanted to see his own metrics. The architectural decision that made it succeed: separate the visualization layer from the data source. Any backend can be a plugin.

## How it works

Grafana has three main pieces: the panel, the data source, and the dashboard.

A **panel** is a single visualization (a graph, a table, a stat). It knows how to draw itself but not where the data comes from. It asks a data source for a query result, then renders whatever comes back.

A **data source** is a plugin that knows how to talk to one backend. Prometheus has one, InfluxDB has one, and you can write your own. Each implements the same interface: take a query, return time-series data in a standard format.

A **dashboard** is a collection of panels with shared time ranges and variables. Change the time picker and every panel re-queries its data source with the new range.

The plugin model is the leverage. Adding support for a new database does not require changing any visualization code. You write one adapter, and every panel type works with it.

## Build something similar

Start with a web app that renders a chart from one data source. Define a simple interface: `query(range)` returns a list of `(timestamp, value)` pairs.

Add a second data source behind the same interface. The moment you have two, you have the core of Grafana. The third and tenth take the same effort as the second.

The hard part is not the charting. It is designing the query interface wide enough that different backends can implement it without contorting their natural query language.

## Sources

Origin story and architecture are described in the Grafana documentary and podcast interviews linked in the evidence field.

GroupMe is group messaging for phones. You create a group, add people, and everyone sees the same thread. The app runs on smartphones, and members without one can join over SMS.

Group texting in 2010 was a patchwork. Carrier group MMS behaved differently across devices, and adding someone mid-thread often broke the thread. A group that mixed smartphones and basic phones had no shared space.

A communication product is only as useful as its least-equipped member. Supporting the oldest channel in the group can be the feature that makes the rest work.

## What it does

HipHop for PHP converts PHP source into C++ and compiles the result. Facebook ran its PHP web tier through it and reported roughly half the CPU usage for the same work.

## The key insight

Facebook did not want to rewrite the site. The team wanted the existing PHP codebase to run faster without a language migration. HipHop keeps PHP as the source language and moves the cost from request time to build time.

That trade is the whole idea. Compilation is slow and awkward, but it happens once. Interpretation happens on every request.

## How it works

The compiler parses PHP, builds an abstract syntax tree, and generates C++ that calls a runtime library for dynamic behavior. PHP is dynamically typed, so the generated code cannot assume types. The runtime provides the operations that need them: array access, string conversion, method dispatch.

Static analysis recovers what it can. Where a variable's type is provable, the generated C++ uses a concrete type. Where it is not, the code falls back to a generic path. The ratio between the two determines how much speed the build actually buys.

The output is compiled with a normal C++ toolchain and linked against the HipHop runtime. Deployment ships a binary instead of a directory of scripts, which changes the release process as much as it changes performance.

Compatibility is the long tail. PHP's behavior in edge cases is defined by its interpreter, and a reimplementation has to match it closely enough that production code does not change meaning. Each mismatch is a bug that only appears on a specific code path.

The project later gave way to HHVM, a virtual machine with a JIT. That design keeps the dynamic language and recovers speed at runtime, which removed the build step that made HipHop expensive to operate.

## Build something similar

Take a small language or a configuration format and compile it to a language you already run. Start with arithmetic, variables, and function calls.

Generate code, compile it, and compare the output against an interpreter for the same program. Then add one dynamic feature, such as a dictionary with mixed value types, and watch the generated code lose its static types.

That moment shows where the real work lives. The compiler is straightforward. Matching the dynamic semantics is the project.

## Sources

Origin, author, and CPU savings are linked in the evidence field.
projects.description: PHP to C++ compiler that reduced CPU usage by approximately 50%. Open-sourced in February 2010.

evidence.supports: Facebook hackathon origin, Haiping Zhao, CPU savings

projects.key_idea: Translate PHP into C++ ahead of time, so the same code runs without paying interpreter cost per request.
projects.learn_from: A code generator plus a compatibility layer can buy years of headroom while you build the real runtime.
projects.name: HipHop for PHP

## What it does

Hollow Knight is a metroidvania set in a ruined underground kingdom. You play a small knight with a nail, explore interconnected rooms, and unlock movement abilities that open routes you could see but not reach earlier.

## The key insight

The project started as a Ludum Dare 27 entry in 2013, built in a weekend around the theme "ten seconds." What survived from that build was not its content. It was the feel: a small figure moving through a dark, hand-drawn space.

Team Cherry kept that and rebuilt the rest over several years. The jam version proved the tone cheaply. The commercial game needed a much larger map, a combat system, and a save structure, and none of those fit in a weekend.

## How it works

The map is a graph. Each room is a node, each exit is an edge, and most edges are gated by either an ability or a key item. Designers place gates so that the player passes a locked route early and remembers it. Later, a new ability turns the remembered route into progress.

Combat is built on spacing and timing rather than combos. The nail has a short range, the dash moves a fixed distance, and healing takes time during which the player is vulnerable. Every fight is a negotiation between dealing damage and buying the moment to heal.

The charm system is a loadout constraint. Charms modify health, damage, movement, or summon behavior, but you can only equip as many as your notch count allows. The constraint turns a large set of upgrades into a build decision instead of a checklist.

Saving happens at benches. A bench restores health and respawns enemies, so progress and risk are tied to a physical location rather than a menu.

## Build something similar

Start with one room and one movement verb. Make the character move, jump, and attack. Tune the acceleration, the jump arc, and the attack recovery until moving through an empty room feels good on its own.

Then build three rooms with one gate. Put an item behind the gate that the player can see but not reach. Add the ability that opens it. If the return trip feels like a reward rather than a chore, the core loop works.

Add a bench before adding a boss. Saving is the pacing device that makes the rest tolerable.

## Sources

Jam origin and development history are linked in the evidence field.

Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes is a cooperative bomb-defusal game. One player sees a bomb in VR; the others hold a manual and cannot see it.

## The problem

Co-op games usually give every player the same information, which makes coordination a matter of reflexes. This one makes coordination the entire game by splitting the information.

It began as a Global Game Jam 2015 prototype and became one of the best-selling VR titles on Steam. The manual is printable paper, so the game supports any number of players without extra hardware.

Asymmetric information is a cheap source of depth. Before adding mechanics, check whether splitting what players know creates the tension you want.

The record does not describe the bomb-generation logic or how the VR and non-VR versions differ.

## What it is

Landsat Connect is a web app for following Landsat satellites. It shows surface reflectance data and notifies users when a satellite passes over an area.

## The problem

Landsat data is open but not approachable. A researcher or land manager has to know which scene to request and when it was captured.

## What makes it interesting

It won Best Mission Concept at NASA Space Apps 2024. The pass notification turns an archive into a subscription, which is the difference between data being available and being used.

## What you can learn

## What it does

OpenAI Gym is a standard interface for reinforcement learning environments. An agent sees an observation, picks an action, and receives a reward and a new observation. Gym defines the shape of that exchange so the same training loop can drive a cart-pole simulation, an Atari game, or a robot arm.

## The key insight

Before Gym, most papers shipped their own environment code and their own training harness. Results were hard to compare because the loop itself differed between implementations. Gym standardized the environment side of the loop and left the algorithm side alone. That is a much smaller surface than a full framework, and it was enough.

## How it works

Every environment implements the same contract:

- `reset()` returns the first observation.
- `step(action)` returns observation, reward, done, and an info dictionary.
- `action_space` and `observation_space` describe legal actions and observations.

Spaces are typed. `Discrete(4)` is a set of four actions. `Box(low, high, shape)` is a continuous array with bounds. Because the shapes are declared, an algorithm can build the right input and output layers without knowing which environment it is talking to.

Wrappers modify an environment while keeping the contract. Frame stacking, reward scaling, and time limits are all wrappers: they take an environment and return an environment. This is composition instead of configuration, and it is why third-party modifications do not require changes to the core.

Registration maps a string like `CartPole-v1` to a constructor. `gym.make` builds the environment and wraps it. Versioning in the name matters: `v0` and `v1` can differ in reward definition or episode length, and published results cite the version.

## Build something similar

Define the contract first, in fewer than ten lines. Two methods and two space objects are enough.

Build one environment with a trivial dynamic, then write a random agent that samples from the action space and prints the episode return. If the agent can run without importing anything specific to that environment, the interface works.

Then add a wrapper that changes one thing, such as stacking the last four observations. If the wrapper needs no change to the agent, the composition boundary is in the right place.

## Sources

The interface and repository are linked in the evidence field.

evidence.supports: OpenAI Gym repository and docs; OpenAI has stated it was not a formal hackathon project but embodied rapid-build research culture

projects.learn_from: A boring, fixed contract creates an ecosystem. Five methods beat a clever framework.

## What it does

Project Naptha is a browser extension that makes text inside images selectable, copyable, editable, and translatable. You drag over a screenshot or a meme as if it were a document, and the words come out.

## The key insight

Optical character recognition was not new in 2013. The insight was placement. Once the engine returns words with bounding boxes, the extension can position transparent text elements directly over the image. From that point, the browser's own selection, copy, and translation features do the rest.

The interface is the trick. Users do not learn a new tool. They use the selection behavior they already have.

## How it works

The extension captures the image, draws it to a canvas, and runs an OCR engine compiled to JavaScript. Running locally avoids uploading every image to a server, which matters for privacy and for latency.

The engine returns recognized words and their coordinates. The extension creates a layer above the image with one positioned element per word or line. The text is transparent, but it sits in the same place as the pixels, so a drag selects the words under the cursor.

Because the layer is real text, other features follow. Copy puts the words on the clipboard. A translation action sends the selected string to a translation service. An edit action hides the original region and draws a replacement.

Detection is the weak point. OCR on low-resolution or stylized text produces garbage, so the extension scores confidence and only builds overlays where the result is plausible. Images without text get no layer.

## Build something similar

Take one screenshot with clear text. Run any OCR engine over it and print each word with its bounding box.

Draw absolutely positioned spans over the image using those boxes, with transparent color. Select them with the mouse. If selection lands on the right words, the core mechanism works.

Then handle failure. Rotate the image, blur it, and use a decorative font. Decide what confidence threshold means "no text here" rather than producing nonsense.

## Sources

HackMIT origin is linked in the evidence field.

## What it does

Sphero makes connected rolling robots, including the BB-8 toy. The product is a sealed sphere that drives, lights up, and is controlled from a phone.

## The key insight

The robot is deliberately dumb. It contains motors, a battery, a radio, and enough firmware to execute commands. The phone holds the interface, the games, and the behavior logic.

That split means new behavior ships as an app update. The hardware does not need to be redesigned when someone invents a new way to use it, and the bill of materials stays low because the device carries no display and no general-purpose compute.

## How it works

Inside the sphere, two wheels drive against the inner shell. Steering comes from the difference in wheel speeds, and the center of mass sits low so the robot self-rights. A sphere with two driven wheels has no front, which is why the robot can move in any direction without turning first.

An inertial measurement unit reports orientation and acceleration. The firmware uses it to hold a heading and to report collisions. The phone uses it to render motion and to score games.

The radio link carries short commands: set speed, set color, play a sound, read sensors. The protocol is small because the device is not streaming video or running a language runtime. Latency matters more than bandwidth, since the user is steering.

The SDK exposes those commands to third-party developers. Sphero's educational line leans on the same idea: the robot is an output device, and the programming happens in an app or a block-based editor.

## Build something similar

Build a two-wheeled robot in a clear sphere, or simulate one. Expose three commands over a wireless link: drive with a heading and speed, set an LED color, read the IMU.

Put the control loop on the phone. Draw a joystick, map it to a heading and speed, and send the command at a fixed rate.

Then add one behavior that lives entirely in the app, such as a patrol route or a reaction to being picked up. If you can change that behavior without touching firmware, the split is working.

## The key insight

The team did not set out to build a shooter. They set out to make something in seven days. The time-movement mechanic emerged from a jam constraint: make one interesting rule and build everything around it.

The mechanic does double duty. It is a puzzle rule (position yourself before time advances) and a difficulty dial (move less, survive longer). Every level design problem becomes "what does the player need to do while frozen?"

## How it works

The simulation runs on a fixed timestep, but the timestep only advances when the player provides input. The engine has two states: frozen (delta time = 0) and running (delta time = normal).

When frozen, physics does not integrate, AI does not tick, and particles pause. Bullets keep their positions because velocity integrates against delta time. Zero delta time freezes them in place.

When the player moves (WASD or mouse look), the engine switches to running. One frame of input produces one frame of simulation. When the player stops, the engine drops back to frozen.

The bullet freezing comes for free. No special-casing required: the mechanic falls out of the physics loop.

Level design is the real work. Each arena is laid out so the optimal solution involves specific movement sequences: dodge here, shoot there, reposition. The levels teach the mechanic through geometry, not tutorials.

## Build something similar

Start with a simple FPS scene: a player controller, a few enemies that shoot, and bullets that travel.

Add a pause system. When the player is not pressing movement keys, set time scale to 0. When they press a key, set it back to 1.

Test it: fire a shot, release all keys, watch the bullet stop mid-air.

Then design three arenas around the mechanic. The first should be trivial (stand still, aim, move to shoot). The second should require repositioning between shots. The third should punish standing still (enemies close in over time).

## Sources

Prototype origin and development timeline are documented at superhotgame.com/our-story, linked in the evidence field.

## What it is

Trello organizes work into boards, lists, and cards. A card is a task; moving it between lists shows progress. The board is a kanban wall that a team can read without training.

## The problem

Project tools of the time were built around fields, filters, and reports. A small team that wanted to see who was doing what had to configure a system before using it. Trello's bet was that the board metaphor already existed in offices, on walls and sticky notes.

## What makes it interesting

It came out of Fog Creek's Creek Weeks, an internal hack-week format where employees pitched and prototyped products. The prototype was pitched in January 2011 and the product launched at TechCrunch Disrupt that September. Closing that gap is the part most hack-week projects never manage.

## What you can learn

A familiar physical object is a cheaper interface than a new vocabulary. If users can guess where to click, onboarding is mostly done.

## Limitations of this analysis

The record documents the origin and launch, not the implementation. Trello's data model, sync approach, and early scaling work are not covered by the linked sources.

## What it is

Ushahidi is an open-source platform for collecting eyewitness reports and placing them on a map. Reports arrive by SMS or the web and appear as points that responders can filter.

## The problem

During the 2008 post-election violence in Kenya, information was spread across blogs, news, and phone calls. There was no shared map of what was happening where.

## How the experience works

A report is sent by text message or submitted online. The platform geocodes it, adds it to the map, and lets moderators review and categorize it. The map is the interface; the reports are the data.

## What makes it interesting

Four technologists built it in days as an ad hoc response, not a planned product. It won the NetSquared Mashup Challenge in 2008 and became a platform used in later crises. The SMS input was the key choice: the people closest to an event often have the weakest connection.

## What you can learn

When the network is unreliable, the input channel decides whether the tool works at all. Design for the phone people have, not the one you wish they had.

## Limitations of this analysis

The record does not cover the moderation workflow, verification methods, or later versions of the platform.

## What it does

Zapier connects over 7,000 web applications. A Zap is a trigger (new email, new row, new file) paired with an action (create a task, send a message, add a row) in a different app. When the trigger fires, Zapier performs the action.

## The key insight

Zapier started at a Startup Weekend in Columbia, Missouri in October 2011. Wade Foster, Mike Knoop, and Bryan Vance built a demo that connected two apps in a weekend. The insight that turned it into a company: every app has an API, but most app pairs do not have a direct integration. A middleware layer that translates between thousands of APIs is more valuable than building any single integration.

The product is not any one Zap. It is the platform that lets a non-developer create the next thousand without writing code.

## How it works

**Trigger.** Zapier polls an app's API (or receives a webhook) for new events. When a new Gmail arrives, a new row appears in Sheets, or a new file lands in Dropbox, the trigger fires.

**Mapping.** The user defines which fields from the trigger map to which fields in the action. Gmail Subject becomes Slack Message Text. This is a simple key-value transformation.

**Action.** Zapier calls the target app's API with the mapped data. If the API returns an error, Zapier retries with exponential backoff.

**Polling vs webhooks.** Some apps support webhooks (push). Others only support polling (pull). Zapier handles both; the user does not know which is happening.

The engineering challenge is coverage. Each of the 7,000 apps has its own auth scheme, rate limits, pagination style, and error format. Zapier maintains an adapter for each. The platform value grows with every adapter added.

## Build something similar

Build a mini-Zapier that connects two apps you use daily.

Pick a trigger app with a simple API (GitHub: new commit, or RSS feed: new item). Pick an action app with a simple API (Slack: post message, or Notion: create page).

Write a script that polls the trigger every 60 seconds, checks for new items since the last poll, and calls the action API for each new item. Store the last-seen timestamp in a file.

This is one Zap. The platform insight comes when you abstract the trigger and action behind interfaces and let users define the mapping. The second and third Zaps take the same code as the first.

## Sources

Startup Weekend origin is documented in Silicon Prairie News and Inc. articles linked in the evidence field.

## What it is

zkPow is a zero-knowledge system for proving work reputation without revealing the underlying data.

## The problem

A reputation score is only useful if it can be checked. Sharing the raw history to prove it exposes information the person may not want to disclose.

It won the ZK and Privacy category at ETH Porto 2023. The project separates the claim from the evidence, which is the core promise of a proof system.

## What you can learn

Privacy is a feature of verification, not its opposite. A proof that reveals nothing can be more convincing than a document that reveals everything.

## Limitations of this analysis

The record does not describe the circuit, the reputation model, or the cost of proving.
